summary: Jesus heals a man's withered hand on the Sabbath while his opponents watch to see if he will, and the moment he does they start planning to kill him — six verses in. Crowds then arrive from every direction, he appoints twelve men as an inner circle, and the chapter closes with two verdicts on him from opposite sides: his own family says he is out of his mind and comes to take him home, while scribes from Jerusalem say he is working for the devil. He answers both, and redefines who counts as family.
whyItMatters: This is where the book stops being about a popular healer. Within one chapter Jesus is the target of a death plot, is declared insane by his relatives, and is accused of demonic collaboration by the authorities. The pressure that ends at the cross starts here.

context.author: Anonymous; early tradition names Mark, recording Peter's preaching
context.audience: Non-Jewish readers — note that Mark stops to translate the nickname 'Boanerges' in verse 17
context.setting: A Galilean synagogue, the lakeshore, a mountain, and a crowded house
context.literaryForm: Narrative with Mark's signature sandwich — the family story is split open and the Beelzebul charge is set inside it

keyVerses.text: When he had looked around at them with anger, being grieved at the hardening of their hearts
keyVerses.why: One of the few places any gospel names Jesus's anger outright. Mark also names the grief underneath it.

keyVerses.text: The Pharisees went out, and immediately conspired with the Herodians against him, how they might destroy him.
keyVerses.why: The death plot appears in chapter 3 of 16. Everything after this happens under that shadow.

keyVerses.text: But no one can enter into the house of the strong man to plunder unless he first binds the strong man
keyVerses.why: His own account of what the exorcisms are: not skirmishes, a break-in already in progress.

keyVerses.text: For whoever does the will of God is my brother, my sister, and mother.
keyVerses.why: Family redrawn around allegiance rather than blood — spoken while his actual family waits outside.

questions.question: Why is healing someone a Sabbath violation?
questions.answer: Healing counted as work, and the accepted position allowed it on the Sabbath only when a life was in danger. A withered hand is not an emergency — the man could have come back the next day. That is what makes it a test. Jesus reframes the question in verse 4: if you can choose to do good or to do harm, is postponing good actually neutral? Nobody answers him.

questions.question: Jesus gets angry. Is that unusual?
questions.answer: It is rare enough to notice. Mark says he looked around at them with anger, grieved at the hardening of their hearts — and Matthew and Luke both drop the anger when they retell this scene, which tells you it struck later writers as strong. Mark keeps it, and pairs it with grief. The anger is at people who would rather see a man stay crippled than lose an argument.

questions.question: Who are the Herodians, and why does it matter that the Pharisees teamed up with them?
questions.answer: Supporters of Herod Antipas, the Rome-appointed ruler of Galilee — a political faction, not a religious one. The Pharisees were a devout renewal movement with no love for Herod's court. These two groups had little reason to cooperate on anything. Mark's point in putting them in the same sentence is that Jesus has managed to unite people who agree on nothing else.

questions.question: Why twelve? Is the number meaningful?
questions.answer: Almost certainly. Israel was founded as twelve tribes, and by this period most of them had long since been scattered. Appointing exactly twelve men reads as a deliberate claim: this is Israel being restarted. Mark doesn't spell that out, but the number would not have been lost on his sources.

questions.question: Verse 21 says his family thought he was insane. Does that really say what it looks like?
questions.answer: Yes, and it is one of the bluntest verses in the gospels. The Greek phrase covers his relatives or close associates, and the verb for what they came to do is forceful — to seize or take charge of him. Verse 31 identifies who arrived: his mother and brothers. Matthew and Luke both leave this episode out. Mark keeps it, and then makes it the frame for the accusation that follows.

questions.question: Who or what is Beelzebul?
questions.answer: A name for the prince of demons — Satan, in the scribes' usage here. It appears to derive from an old title meaning something like 'lord of the high place' or, in a mocking variant, 'lord of the flies,' attached to a Philistine god (2 Kings 1:2). The charge is not that Jesus is a fraud. They concede the exorcisms are real and argue about the source of the power.

questions.question: What is the 'strong man' about?
questions.answer: It is Jesus's counter-argument and his own description of what he is doing. If you find a strong man's house being looted, the obvious explanation is not that he is robbing himself — it is that somebody stronger tied him up first. Applied here: the exorcisms are not Satan divided against himself, they are evidence that Satan has already been overpowered and the house is being emptied.

questions.question: What is the unforgivable sin, and should I be worried I've committed it?
questions.answer: Verses 28-29 have frightened readers for centuries, so start with what Mark actually attaches it to: verse 30 says he said this 'because they said, He has an unclean spirit.' The sin in view is looking directly at God's Spirit at work — a man freed, a hand restored — and calling it the work of the devil. It is not a swear word, a doubt, or a season of unbelief. It is the settled decision to name good as evil, which by its nature will not seek forgiveness. Readers across traditions have generally observed that anxiety about having committed it is itself evidence to the contrary.

questions.question: Is Jesus rejecting his mother?
questions.answer: He is answering a claim, not disowning a person. His family is outside, sending word in, having come to take him home as someone who has lost his grip. His reply moves the boundary of family from blood to doing the will of God — and the people it includes are the ones sitting on the floor listening. Worth noting that Mark shows the same brothers unconvinced here, and that James, one of them, later leads the church in Jerusalem.

questions.question: Why does Mark split the family story in half and stuff the Beelzebul argument inside it?
questions.answer: Because he wants you to read them against each other. It is his signature technique — start a story, interrupt it, finish it — and he uses it at least three more times (5:21-43, 11:12-25, 14:53-72). Here the two halves make one point: two very different groups, his own relatives and the religious authorities from the capital, look at the same man and both conclude something is badly wrong with him. Insider status is no help at all.

glossary.def: Backers of Herod Antipas, Rome's client ruler in Galilee. A political faction rather than a religious party.
The nickname Jesus gave James and John. Mark translates it for his readers as 'Sons of Thunder' — a hint at their temperament, and a sign his audience did not know Aramaic.

Attached to one of the Simons in the list. It marks intense devotion to the law and, in this period, sympathy with armed resistance to Rome — which makes the presence of a tax collector in the same group of twelve remarkable.
The surname of Judas. Most likely 'man of Kerioth,' a Judean town, which would make him the only non-Galilean of the Twelve.
The region south of Judea, ancient Edom. Its inclusion in verse 8 shows how far the crowds were travelling.
